I’ve been dancing since I was six, and now at 23, performing with the company is my whole life. But everything changed after the accident last year—my partner fell during rehearsal and I couldn’t move in time. He crushed my leg, and I saw his face break. I still see it. After that, I couldn’t rest. For two months, I was wired—dancing through pain, buying shoes I didn’t need, six pairs in a week, charging them even though I knew I couldn’t pay. I didn’t need sleep; I felt unstoppable, like my body was made of lightning. 

Then it crashed. For the last three months, I can’t feel anything. I stand at the barre and joy is just a word. I lie awake for hours, mind foggy, like I'm underwater. Sometimes, standing on the rooftop after rehearsal, I get this sudden urge—I could just step forward. No plan, just the pull.

But here’s the thing—the agitation, the insomnia, the impulses—they don’t come and go. They’ve been there since the fall. They’re tied to it. Every noise, every touch, throws me back there. I’m not cycling. I’m stuck.
D008-D018_h024.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008-D018_h025.question:
I’m a 23-year-old professional ballet dancer, and things have been unraveling since the accident last year—my partner and I were in a serious car crash, and he didn’t make it. I survived, but ever since, I can’t quiet my mind. I keep reliving the moment—the sound of the impact, the silence after. For about two months afterward, I was running on pure adrenaline. I wasn’t sleeping much, but I didn’t need to—I was choreographing at 3 a.m., buying expensive costumes and equipment online nonstop, maxing out my cards. I felt unstoppable, like I could dance forever. But it wasn’t joy—it felt like I was being pushed, driven by something inside I couldn’t control.

Then, everything crashed. For the past three months, I’ve been drowning. I can’t get out of bed, even for rehearsals. I sleep 12 hours and still feel exhausted. Focusing on steps? Impossible. My mind drifts, and sometimes I catch myself thinking, *I wish I hadn’t survived*. What terrifies me is that these surges of energy and the crashes—they’re not coming out of nowhere. They started *after* the crash, and they’re tied to it. Every panic, every flashback, every sleepless night—they all point back to *that moment*.
D008-D018_h025.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder
